Compression represents the same source with fewer stored or transmitted bits. Lossless coding reconstructs every source value. Lossy coding permits controlled changes and should be evaluated for its intended use. The ZIP illustration is a separate deterministic demonstration using a repeated sentence, not an EEG benchmark result. The exact original and ZIP byte lengths are generated locally and round-trip recovery is checked. The bar chart uses the full uncompressed size scale. Compression ratios depend on the source. General background: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1951

These are the technique families in the website. Huffman coding and ZIP are general-purpose lossless ideas; PNG applies lossless coding to images. DEFLATE combines LZ77 string matching with Huffman coding. MP3 is perceptual audio coding, not an EEG compressor. Mu-law companding is invertible before quantization: the loss comes from subsequently using finitely many levels. PNG is lossless; JPEG is normally lossy. Thresholding and dithering can map grayscale to one bit per pixel; bit packing and file coding are still needed to store it compactly.

EEG is non-invasive scalp recording. Each channel measures voltage relative to another location or reference; it is not an isolated neuron's output or a direct reading of thoughts. Amplification, filtering and analog-to-digital conversion produce sampled multichannel time series. Scalp position and reference affect the measurements. Frequency content, changes across channels and responses aligned to stimuli provide different analysis features. Prolonged recording can support detection of intermittent abnormal activity in conditions such as epilepsy. NICE NG217, recommendation 1.2.10, advises considering ambulatory EEG for up to 48 hours when routine and sleep-deprived EEG are normal but diagnostic uncertainty remains. This motivates longer recordings; it is not a recommendation that all disease detection requires prolonged EEG. Source: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng217/chapter/diagnosis-and-assessment-of-epilepsy .

This slide reviews two established EEG compression families. Linear predictive coding uses a weighted sum of previous samples to predict the next sample. An autoregressive model writes the current sample as that weighted sum plus an innovation or prediction residual. LPC and AR are closely related descriptions of linear prediction, not two independent guarantees of lossless coding. A lossless predictive codec preserves everything required to reproduce the predictor and encodes the residuals without loss. Reversible arithmetic or matched deterministic prediction is required for exact source recovery; fitting an AR model alone is not compression and storing only AR coefficients is not lossless. Memon, Kong and Cinkler (1999) study context-based lossless and near-lossless EEG coding using prediction; quantizing residuals would instead permit error. For transform coding, the discrete cosine transform (DCT) represents a block with cosine components. The discrete wavelet transform (DWT) uses wavelets across scales and time. These transforms can be inverted before coefficients are quantized or removed. Distortion enters through coefficient quantization, thresholding or other information removal. The remaining symbols are then entropy coded. Higgins et al. (2013) study wavelet coefficient quantization and thresholding. Dao, Li and Do (2015), the user-supplied EEG Compression paper, review transform-based lossy methods. This project compares a simple DCT codec with uniform and mu-law quantization; it does not implement LPC, AR or DWT codecs. Sources: https://doi.org/10.1109/4233.788586 ; https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compbiomed.2013.02.011 ; https://doi.org/10.1109/ATC.2015.7388309 .

Preserving downstream recognition after compression is established work, not a novelty claim for this project. Zhang and colleagues combine DCT, personalized neural reconstruction and nonuniform quantization, and evaluate SSVEP recognition after reconstruction. Strypsteen and Bertrand jointly optimize source coding and an inference network for motor execution in an emulated wireless sensor network; this is not the same motor-imagery task used here. BrainCodec studies learned EEG/iEEG compression, including downstream and expert evaluations. The narrower question asks how several simple compressors affect three tasks when the existing original-data decoder remains frozen. These neural codecs are outside the implemented benchmark.

The first bullet states the goal of task-aware compression as a field: optimize a downstream task metric subject to a storage allowance, beyond relying only on compression ratio or percentage root-mean-square difference (PRD). Some existing methods learn coding and inference jointly; other studies evaluate task preservation after reconstruction. This benchmark does not optimize codecs with task labels. Codec settings minimize waveform MSE within each byte cap, and the fixed decoders are then used to measure the resulting task score loss.

Three broad paradigms were selected rather than several variants of one task. SSVEP identifies one of four visual flicker targets. Motor imagery distinguishes imagined left/right hand movements. P300 detects a target flash using the brief response after a stimulus; this is single-flash detection, not complete spelling accuracy. Different features may react differently to quantization or removal of frequency components. Comparing the same people and stored montage reduces confounds, while baseline difficulty and decoder design still differ.
The question is stated in one sentence at equal storage allowance across compressors. SSVEP is a stimulus-driven sustained response to visual flicker; motor imagery is an internally generated imagined action associated with changes in sensorimotor rhythms; P300 detection is based on a transient response aligned to a target event. These represent distinct BCI paradigms and signal features, rather than minor variants of one task. They are not an exhaustive taxonomy of EEG applications. Dataset and paradigm source: https://doi.org/10.1093/gigascience/giz002.
SSVEP is expanded on the slide as steady-state visual evoked potential. This is the sustained response to periodic visual stimulation. Source: https://doi.org/10.1093/gigascience/giz002 .

Evaluation subjects are S07–S26, selected in advance. S03–S06 remain the separate pilot and S01–S02 are development checks. The input has the same twelve channels for every task. Continuous recordings are resampled to 128 Hz and filtered from 0.5 to 40 Hz. The split is chronological at 60 percent of events. Training epochs finish two seconds before the boundary, and test epochs begin two seconds after it. Filtering is offline and noncausal, which remains a limitation. SSVEP and MI epochs last four seconds; P300 epochs last one second. Overlapping P300 test epochs share a single encoded continuous recording. One-second codec frames choose the least waveform MSE among a predefined candidate grid that fits each cap, without labels or classifier outcomes. Decoders and event annotations are outside EEG payload for every method. Raw selected float32 requires 512 bytes/s/channel. Balanced accuracy averages recall across classes; chance is 25 percent for SSVEP and 50 percent for MI/P300. Each person's score receives equal weight. CCA uses known frequency templates. CSP is a learned spatial filter; LDA is linear discriminant analysis. Alternative decoders are fixed in advance, calibrated on original early data and never adapted to compression. Both P300 decoders share the same low-frequency time-bin features. A float32+ZIP control must recover exact samples and preserve predictions.

At 32 bytes/s/channel, primary mean losses are 12.13/9.22/9.47 pp for uniform, 12.95/10.91/9.60 for mu-law, and 8.82/4.10/0.61 for DCT, ordered SSVEP/MI/P300. All primary SSVEP-minus-MI paired intervals cross zero at this cap. SSVEP is the largest-loss task for only eight of twenty people under uniform, despite its largest group mean. Changing decoders changes the task ordering. The strongest repeated local result is P300's DCT advantage over uniform: 8.87 pp with interval 7.95–9.83 for the primary decoder, and 10.05 pp with interval 9.00–11.20 for the alternative. Every new participant shows that direction. Both P300 decoders use the same low-frequency features, so this does not test all P300 analysis methods. P300 DCT changes about 5.9 percent of primary predictions despite only 0.61 pp mean score loss; correct-to-incorrect and incorrect-to-correct changes can partly cancel. Baseline difficulty matters: primary SSVEP still scores about 81 percent under tight-cap uniform while MI is about 61 percent against a 50 percent chance level.

The extension improves the sample size but still uses a fixed, nonrandom subset of one acquisition study. A new day, real-time deployment, clinical interpretation and device power were not tested. The continuous noncausal filter can couple neighboring samples across the split despite the epoch guard. Original task difficulty differs, and weak baselines are retained. Each task has only two chosen decoders. The alternative P300 decoder changes the classifier but not the features, so a broader feature comparison is still needed. All codec settings were selected using waveform MSE, not task labels, but their search grids differ. Equal maximum byte caps leave different unused space. Future work should test more datasets and tasks, independently varied feature extractors, stronger EEG codecs and more closely matched achieved rates. Streaming and hardware experiments would be needed for latency or battery claims.
The fourth visible limitation explicitly states that state of the art EEG codecs and compressors were not tested. Broader compressor comparisons are a future step.
